text:
Kira Thompson: quick q for security/compliance folks re: post-incident summary redaction. we’re drafting the customer-facing summary for the streaming degradation last week and got hung up on:
1) wording when it’s a cloud/provider issue
2) how to talk about “customer-specific” impacts (one big tenant had it worse)

Trying to keep it useful but not overshare. @Dr. Aisha Rahman @Olga Petrov @Michael Grant any guidance / examples?

Rafael Mendes: +1. also: can we say “AWS”/“GCP” explicitly or should it always be “upstream provider”? and can we mention it was isolated to us-east-1?

Sean Gallagher: following. we keep getting “who was impacted” questions from enterprise, but we also don’t want to accidentally disclose tenant info in a public summary.

Dr. Aisha Rahman: yep, good questions. baseline: public summaries should be actionable + honest, but avoid anything that increases attack surface or reveals customer identities/contractual specifics.

Dr. Aisha Rahman: on provider issues:
- default: “an upstream cloud provider” / “an upstream networking provider” (don’t name unless comms/legal has explicitly approved naming for that incident)
- it’s OK to mention region(s) impacted (us-east/us-west/eu-west) if it’s already customer-observable + helps customers route/fallback
- don’t include provider ticket IDs, exact AZ, IP ranges, router vendor, BGP details, etc.

Olga Petrov: +1. also: some of our provider agreements prefer we don’t attribute outages publicly. safer to say “upstream provider” unless Legal says otherwise.

Michael Grant: from legal/privacy side: avoid naming customers, avoid “only Customer X” / “top 3 enterprise customers” etc. even “a single large customer” can be identifying depending on context.

Kira Thompson: makes sense. what about describing severity skew? in the internal PM we had “Enterprise tenant A was 30-40% errors due to pinned region + high concurrency.”

Marcus Lin: security angle: also avoid describing “why that tenant was worse” if it exposes their configuration choices. you can say “a subset of traffic patterns experienced higher error rates” without calling out the pattern if it’s uniquely identifying.

Tomáš Novák: in the summary template we have “Customer impact” + “Workarounds.” How specific can we be on workaround? e.g., “switch to model X in us-west” vs “change config Y in Dedicated”?

Dr. Aisha Rahman: workaround guidance is OK as long as it’s generally applicable and not tied to a specific customer’s setup.
Examples that are OK:
- “If you are pinned to us-east, consider temporarily routing to us-west or eu-west.”
- “Retry with exponential backoff for intermittent 5xx.”
- “If streaming responses are failing, you can use non-streaming responses as a temporary workaround.”

Dr. Aisha Rahman: Examples to avoid:
- “Customer <name> should remove header <X>”
- “If you’re using the <internal feature flag name>…”
- “Disable <security control> to mitigate”

Rafael Mendes: ok. can we say “some customers saw elevated disconnects on streaming” + “non-streaming unaffected”? (that’s what support wants)

Olga Petrov: yes, that’s the kind of granularity we want. just avoid any counts that could be used to infer a customer. “subset of requests” is fine.

Elliot Price: docs side: we’re updating macros too. would love a “blessed” set of phrases for provider issues + partial impact.

Kira Thompson: can we propose a canned phrasing block? something like:

"Root cause: An upstream cloud networking provider experienced intermittent packet loss affecting a subset of traffic to our us-east serving cluster."

Is “packet loss” too specific?

Marcus Lin: “packet loss” is usually OK, but don’t go further into mechanism (BGP flap, route leak, specific router model, etc). If it was actually a capacity issue or load balancer bug, keep it at “upstream networking disruption” / “upstream networking instability.”

Dr. Aisha Rahman: agree. “packet loss” is borderline but generally acceptable if it’s accurate and already apparent from symptoms (disconnects/timeouts). If there’s any uncertainty, use “network instability.”

Sean Gallagher: what about timelines? internal has exact times to the minute. do we publish minute-level? customers asked.

Olga Petrov: minute-level is fine and helpful (start/mitigated/resolved). Avoid including internal detection tooling names or pages. Just keep it to “09:12–10:03 UTC” style.

Michael Grant: +1. time is not sensitive. but don’t paste raw logs.

Kira Thompson: ok. second question: “customer-specific impacts.” What’s a safe way to acknowledge skew without calling out the customer?

Dr. Aisha Rahman: safe patterns:
- “A subset of customers with traffic pinned to us-east experienced higher error rates.”
- “Impact varied by workload and request volume; the highest-traffic workloads saw elevated streaming disconnects.”
- “A small subset of requests experienced errors” (if you really need to keep it vague)

Dr. Aisha Rahman: avoid:
- “A single enterprise customer…”
- “Customers in healthcare…” (industry can be identifying)
- “Customer with dedicated capacity pool <X>…”

Rafael Mendes: what about quantifying %? e.g., “streaming error rate peaked at 12% in us-east.” is that ok?

Olga Petrov: yes, aggregate metrics are good. just make sure it’s not per-customer. “peaked at X% of streaming requests in us-east” is fine.

Marcus Lin: sanity check: ensure the metric is truly aggregate and not “top tenant” derived. if it’s from a top-N dashboard, don’t publish.

Tomáš Novák: in the prevention section, can we say “added alert for upstream provider latency” or is that implying details?

Dr. Aisha Rahman: you can say “improved monitoring and automated failover for upstream dependency health” and “added region-level detection for streaming disconnects.” Keep it outcome-focused.

Elliot Price: can you drop a couple approved example sentences we can reuse across summaries? (helps docs + support macros)

Dr. Aisha Rahman: sure, here are a few “approved-ish” options (still do a quick review for Sev0/Sev1):
1) Provider issue:
- “An upstream cloud provider experienced a service disruption that affected connectivity to our us-east serving cluster.”
- “An upstream dependency issue led to elevated timeouts for a subset of requests in us-east.”

2) Partial impact / streaming-only:
- “Streaming responses experienced elevated disconnects; non-streaming responses and embeddings were not impacted.”
- “Some customers experienced increased latency and intermittent errors on the Streaming component.”

3) Skew / subset:
- “Impact varied by traffic patterns; customers pinned to us-east were more likely to experience errors.”

4) Mitigation:
- “We mitigated by shifting traffic to healthy capacity and increasing connection keepalive thresholds.” (only if that’s not sensitive and is accurate)

Michael Grant: +1 to those. avoid “keepalive thresholds” if it reveals a security or anti-abuse control. but generally it’s fine if it’s operational.

Kira Thompson: super helpful. last: if we need to mention a “single customer experienced prolonged impact” because they were pinned + had strict timeouts, can we handle via private follow-up only?

Sean Gallagher: please yes. we can do 1:1 comms via CSM for that account.

Olga Petrov: correct. public summary should stay aggregate. for individual customers: CSM/support can share more specifics privately, still following NDA + least-privilege.

Rafael Mendes: action item: Kira can you update the summary draft to replace provider name with “upstream provider” and remove the tenant callout? I’ll route to @Dr. Aisha Rahman for quick look.

Kira Thompson: yep. will post draft in #incidents-review too. thanks all.

Elliot Price: I’ll take the example phrases and incorporate into the docs PR + support macro draft. :thumbsup:

Dr. Aisha Rahman: sounds good. if anything feels borderline, err on general + actionable. happy to review.

Marcus Lin: also: if root cause touches security (e.g., abuse traffic, WAF changes, auth anomalies), pull me in before publish.

Kira Thompson: noted. :+1:

Rafael Mendes: closing loop: we should add this to the “redaction checklist” section in the template (provider naming + customer skew language). @Tomáš Novák can you capture in runbook?

Tomáš Novák: yep, will add a bullet list + examples to the runbook page and link it from the summary workflow.

Sean Gallagher: thanks all. this will save us a bunch of back-and-forth next time.
